goals: State where glycolysis and the Krebs cycle take place and what each produces

slides.heading: Respiration in Plants
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how every living cell of a plant releases the energy locked in food.

visual.alt: Flow from glucose through respiration to energy for life processes

slides.narration: A plant makes food in its leaves, but food is of no use until the energy in it is released. That release is respiration, and it goes on all day and all night in every living cell, in roots, stems, leaves and seeds.

slides.heading: Respiration is not breathing

rows: At the surface of the organism
Food is broken down to release energy
Gases are exchanged with the surroundings
Energy, carbon dioxide, water or alcohol
Oxygen taken in, carbon dioxide given out

visual.alt: Table distinguishing respiration inside cells from gas exchange at the surface

slides.narration: Do not confuse respiration with breathing. Respiration is a chemical process inside the cell that releases energy from food. Gas exchange is only the way oxygen reaches the cell and carbon dioxide leaves it.

slides.heading: Where respiration happens
slides.body_md: Glucose is first broken down in the **cytoplasm**; the breakdown is finished in the **mitochondrion**.

slides.narration: In the fluid of the cell, glucose is split into a smaller substance called pyruvate. With oxygen present, pyruvate moves into a mitochondrion, where it is broken down completely. Without oxygen, the cell makes alcohol and carbon dioxide instead.

slides.heading: Glycolysis and the Krebs cycle

rows: Two pyruvate and a little energy
Carbon dioxide, water and much more energy

visual.alt: Table comparing glycolysis and the Krebs cycle for site, oxygen need, starting substance and products

slides.narration: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm and does not need oxygen. It splits one glucose into two pyruvate and releases a little energy. The Krebs cycle happens in the mitochondria and needs oxygen. It releases carbon dioxide, water and most of the energy.

slides.heading: Quick check: the site of glycolysis
slides.narration: Where does glucose first meet the enzymes?

slides.heading: Aerobic respiration
slides.body_md: Aerobic respiration uses **oxygen** and breaks glucose down **completely**.

visual.alt: Aerobic respiration: one glucose and six oxygen give six carbon dioxide, six water and energy

slides.narration: In aerobic respiration, one glucose molecule reacts with six molecules of oxygen to give six molecules of carbon dioxide and six of water, and a large amount of energy. It is the usual kind of respiration in plants.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: aerobic respiration of five glucose molecules
slides.body_md: 5 glucose molecules are respired aerobically. How many oxygen molecules are used, and how many carbon dioxide and water molecules are made?
bullets: Step 1: one glucose uses 6 oxygen, so 5 × 6 = **30**.
Step 2: one glucose makes 6 carbon dioxide, so 5 × 6 = **30**.
Step 3: one glucose makes 6 water, so 5 × 6 = **30**.

visual.alt: Worked table: thirty oxygen used, thirty carbon dioxide and thirty water made for five glucose

slides.narration: Read the numbers from the equation for one glucose and multiply by five. Six oxygen each gives thirty. Six carbon dioxide each gives thirty. Six water each gives thirty.

slides.heading: Anaerobic respiration
slides.body_md: In plants and yeast, anaerobic respiration works **without oxygen** and gives **alcohol**.

visual.alt: Anaerobic respiration: one glucose gives two ethanol, two carbon dioxide and a little energy

slides.narration: Without oxygen, one glucose molecule is only partly broken down. It gives two molecules of alcohol and two of carbon dioxide, and releases much less energy. Yeast and roots in waterlogged soil respire in this way.

slides.heading: Aerobic and anaerobic compared

visual.alt: Table comparing aerobic and anaerobic respiration in oxygen, breakdown, end products, energy and site

slides.narration: Aerobic respiration needs oxygen, breaks glucose down completely, and gives carbon dioxide and water with a large amount of energy. Anaerobic respiration needs no oxygen and gives alcohol and carbon dioxide with only a small amount of energy.

slides.heading: Quick check: alcohol
slides.body_md: In plants, anaerobic respiration of glucose gives carbon dioxide and
slides.narration: Think of what yeast makes in fermentation.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: anaerobic respiration of eight glucose molecules
slides.body_md: 8 glucose molecules are respired without oxygen. How many alcohol and carbon dioxide molecules are made?
bullets: Step 1: one glucose gives 2 alcohol, so 8 × 2 = **16**.
Step 2: one glucose gives 2 carbon dioxide, so 8 × 2 = **16**.

visual.alt: Worked table: sixteen alcohol molecules and sixteen carbon dioxide molecules from eight glucose

slides.narration: Use the anaerobic equation for one glucose. It gives two alcohol and two carbon dioxide. Multiply each by eight and you get sixteen of each.

slides.heading: Quick check: the larger energy yield
slides.body_md: Which kind of respiration releases more energy from each glucose molecule?
slides.narration: Complete breakdown releases more.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Glycolysis: cytoplasm, glucose to pyruvate, no oxygen needed.
Krebs cycle: mitochondria, needs oxygen, gives carbon dioxide, water and most of the energy.
Aerobic: more energy; anaerobic in plants: alcohol, carbon dioxide and little energy.

visual.alt: Summary table of aerobic and anaerobic respiration

slides.narration: To recap. Glucose is first split in the cytoplasm by glycolysis. With oxygen the Krebs cycle in the mitochondria finishes the job and releases a lot of energy. Without oxygen plants make alcohol and carbon dioxide and release only a little energy.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write the equations **balanced**, with **energy** on the right.
Name the **site**: glycolysis in the **cytoplasm**, Krebs cycle in the **mitochondria**.
Do not call respiration **breathing**.
In comparisons, give a **matching point** for each side.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Write equations balanced and show energy on the right. Name the site of each stage. Never call respiration breathing. And in a comparison, give a matching point for aerobic and for anaerobic respiration.

decks.title: Respiration in Plants — Part 2: Gaseous exchange and experiments on respiration
goals: Describe how plants exchange gases and how respiration differs from photosynthesis
Describe an experiment showing that germinating seeds give out carbon dioxide
Describe the thermos-flask experiment for heat and explain the need for a control

slides.heading: Gaseous Exchange and Experiments
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how gases move in plants, and how we can prove that seeds respire.

visual.alt: Flow from oxygen in, to respiration, to carbon dioxide and heat out

slides.narration: Respiration takes in oxygen and gives out carbon dioxide and heat. We cannot see this, so we design experiments that make it visible, using germinating seeds because they respire fast.

slides.heading: Gaseous exchange in plants

rows: Oxygen in and carbon dioxide out (reverse in light, for photosynthesis)
Oxygen in and carbon dioxide out
Oxygen from air spaces in the soil

visual.alt: Table of the organs of a plant, their openings and the gases that pass through them

slides.narration: Plants have no lungs. Gases diffuse through tiny pores called stomata in the leaves and young stems, through lenticels in woody stems, and through the surface of the roots, which take oxygen from air spaces in the soil.

slides.heading: Respiration and photosynthesis

visual.alt: Table comparing respiration and photosynthesis

slides.narration: The two processes are opposites. Respiration goes on day and night, uses oxygen and releases energy. Photosynthesis needs light, uses carbon dioxide and stores energy in food. In daylight a green plant gives out more oxygen than it takes in.

slides.narration: Soaked germinating seeds are in flask X. Seeds that were boiled and cooled, which are dead, are in flask Y. Any gas given out passes along the delivery tube into lime water. Lime water turns milky when carbon dioxide is bubbled into it.

slides.heading: The experiment step by step

rows: Put soaked germinating seeds in flask X and an equal mass of boiled, cooled seeds in flask Y
Fit each flask with a cork and a delivery tube dipping into fresh lime water
Leave both flasks for a few hours
Observe the lime water: it turns milky in X but stays clear in Y

visual.alt: Table of four steps in the experiment on carbon dioxide from germinating seeds

slides.narration: Set up both flasks in the same way. After a few hours, the lime water from flask X is milky, which shows that carbon dioxide is given out. The lime water from flask Y, with the dead seeds, stays clear.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading the times
slides.body_md: The lime water turned milky in 36 minutes with 25 g of germinating seeds and in 18 minutes with 50 g. What do the results show?
bullets: Step 1: 50 g is double 25 g, and 36 ÷ 18 = **2**.
Step 2: twice the seeds gave the milky colour in half the time.
Step 3: so more seeds give out carbon dioxide **faster**: the gas comes from respiring seeds.

visual.alt: Worked table: twenty-five grams took thirty-six minutes and fifty grams took eighteen minutes

slides.narration: Compare the two times. Double the mass of seeds took half the time. More living cells means faster respiration and faster release of carbon dioxide.

slides.heading: Quick check: lime water
slides.body_md: Lime water turns milky when which gas is passed through it?
slides.narration: The gas given out in respiration.

slides.heading: Why boiled seeds are the control

rows: Apparatus, mass of seeds, temperature, time
Only whether the seeds are alive
The carbon dioxide in X comes from living seeds, not from air, the flask or the water

visual.alt: Table explaining the control in the carbon dioxide experiment

slides.narration: A control changes only one thing. In flask Y the seeds are dead, so any difference from flask X must be due to life. It shows that the carbon dioxide comes from respiring seeds, and not from the apparatus.

slides.body_md: Respiration also releases **heat**. A vacuum flask keeps the heat in.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: reading the thermometers
slides.body_md: After four days the thermometer in flask A reads 30 degrees and in flask B 22 degrees. Both started at 22 degrees. What do the readings show?
bullets: Step 1: rise in A = 30 − 22 = **8** degrees; rise in B = 22 − 22 = **0**.
Step 2: mean rise in A = 8 ÷ 4 = **2** degrees a day.
Step 3: flask B, the control, did not warm, so the heat in A comes from the **living seeds**.

visual.alt: Worked table of thermometer readings in flasks A and B over four days

slides.narration: The thermometer in flask A climbs by two degrees every day, a rise of eight in all. The control, flask B, does not change. So the heat comes from the respiring seeds.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Gases pass through stomata, lenticels and root surfaces.
Germinating seeds give out carbon dioxide: it turns lime water milky; boiled seeds do not.
Germinating seeds give out heat: the thermometer in the flask of living seeds rises, the control does not.

visual.alt: Summary table of the two experiments with their tests and controls

slides.narration: To recap. Plants exchange gases through stomata, lenticels and roots. Living germinating seeds make lime water milky and warm a vacuum flask. The control with boiled seeds shows no change, which proves the effects come from respiration.

notes.title: Respiration in Plants — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Outline of respiration: glycolysis and the Krebs cycle
sections.body_md:
**Respiration** is the chemical breakdown of food (mainly glucose) in the cells to release energy. It goes on in every living cell, day and night. It is not the same as breathing or gas exchange.

| | Glycolysis | Krebs cycle |
|---|---|---|
| Place | **Cytoplasm** | **Mitochondria** |
| Oxygen | Not needed | Needed |
| Starts with | Glucose (6 carbon atoms) | Pyruvate (3 carbon atoms) |
| Produces | Two **pyruvate** and a little energy | **Carbon dioxide**, **water** and much more energy |

Significance: the energy released is used for growth, active transport, building new substances and other life processes. Without oxygen the Krebs cycle cannot run and the cell is left with the energy from glycolysis alone.

Books differ in how much detail they give; this chapter gives only the outline, and quotes energy as a number of units per glucose (about 36 for aerobic and 2 for anaerobic respiration; some books give 38).

key_terms.definition_md: Breakdown of food in cells to release energy.
Splitting of glucose into two pyruvate in the cytoplasm; no oxygen needed.
Complete breakdown of pyruvate in the mitochondria; needs oxygen.
The cell structure where the Krebs cycle takes place.

sections.heading: 2. Aerobic and anaerobic respiration
sections.body_md:
**Aerobic** (with oxygen): complete breakdown, large energy.

$$\ce{C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy}$$

**Anaerobic** (without oxygen), in plants and yeast: incomplete breakdown, small energy, alcohol (ethanol) is formed.

$$\ce{C6H12O6 -> 2C2H5OH + 2CO2 + energy}$$

| Feature | Aerobic | Anaerobic |
|---|---|---|
| Oxygen | Needed | Not needed |
| Breakdown of glucose | Complete | Incomplete |
| End products | Carbon dioxide and water | Alcohol and carbon dioxide |
| Energy | Large (about 36 units per glucose) | Small (2 units per glucose) |
| Site | Cytoplasm and mitochondria | Cytoplasm |

Anaerobic respiration occurs in yeast (fermentation), in roots in waterlogged soil and in seeds with no air. In animals it gives lactic acid, which is not part of this chapter.

key_terms.definition_md: Respiration that uses oxygen and breaks glucose down completely.
Respiration without oxygen; in plants it gives alcohol and carbon dioxide.
Anaerobic respiration of sugar by yeast.

sections.heading: 3. Gaseous exchange in plants; carbon dioxide from germinating seeds
sections.body_md:
Plants have no lungs; gases move by **diffusion**.
- **Leaves and young stems:** through **stomata**.
- **Woody stems:** through **lenticels**.
- **Roots:** through root hairs and surface cells, taking oxygen from air spaces in the soil.

In light a green plant makes more oxygen by photosynthesis than it uses; in the dark only respiration goes on, so oxygen is taken in and carbon dioxide given out.

**Experiment.** Put soaked germinating seeds in flask X, and the same mass of boiled and cooled (dead) seeds in flask Y. Fit each with a cork and a delivery tube dipping into lime water. After a few hours the lime water in X turns **milky** (carbon dioxide); in Y it stays **clear**. Flask Y is the **control**: only the life of the seeds differs.

key_terms.definition_md: Tiny pores in leaves and young stems for gas exchange.
Small pores in the bark of woody stems for gas exchange.
A clear solution that turns milky with carbon dioxide.

sections.heading: 4. Heat produced in respiration; need for a control
sections.body_md:
Respiration releases some of the energy as **heat**.

**Experiment.** Put soaked germinating seeds in a vacuum (thermos) flask and soaked seeds that were boiled and cooled in a second flask. Close each with cotton wool through which a thermometer passes, with its bulb among the seeds. The cotton wool lets air in but keeps heat. After a few days the thermometer in the flask of living seeds shows a **rise** in temperature; the other does not.

The flask of boiled seeds is the **control**. It is set up in exactly the same way except that the seeds are dead, so it shows that the heat comes from living seeds and not from the surroundings or the apparatus. Both flasks must start at the same temperature and hold the same mass of seeds.

key_terms.definition_md: A set-up identical except for the one factor being tested, used for comparison.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling respiration **breathing**, or writing the equation of photosynthesis by mistake.
- Writing an **unbalanced** equation or leaving out **energy**.
- Forgetting that anaerobic respiration in plants gives **alcohol** (not lactic acid).
- Putting the Krebs cycle in the **cytoplasm**: it is in the **mitochondria**.
- Not naming the **control** (boiled, dead seeds) or not saying why it is needed.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a term, an odd one out **with its category**, a give-reason item.
- 2 marks: two differences or two functions, matched point for point.
- 3 marks: a balanced equation with energy, or three matched points.
- 10-mark structured question: a short situation or diagram with parts of 2 to 4 marks; one part is a labelled diagram.

questions.stem_md: State where glycolysis takes place and what it produces from one glucose molecule.

questions.stem_md: State where the Krebs cycle takes place, whether it needs oxygen and what it produces.

|---|---|

| **No oxygen** needed | **Oxygen** needed |
| Glucose gives **pyruvate** | Pyruvate gives **carbon dioxide and water** |
| **A little** energy | **Much more** energy |

questions.solution_md: Site; oxygen; products; energy.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between respiration and breathing in three points.

3. Respiration goes on in **every living cell**; gas exchange takes place at the **surface** of the organism.

questions.solution_md: Chemical or physical; energy; place.

questions.stem_md: Write the balanced equation for aerobic respiration of glucose.

answer.model_answer_md: C6H12O6 + 6O2 → 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy (glucose and oxygen give carbon dioxide, water and **energy**). The equation is **balanced**: six carbon atoms on each side.

questions.solution_md: Balanced equation with energy.

questions.stem_md: Write the equation for anaerobic respiration in plants and name the two products.

answer.model_answer_md: C6H12O6 → 2C2H5OH + 2CO2 + energy (glucose gives alcohol, carbon dioxide and a little energy). The two products are **alcohol (ethanol)** and **carbon dioxide**, and no oxygen is used.

questions.solution_md: Equation; alcohol and carbon dioxide.

|---|---|

| **Complete** breakdown of glucose | **Incomplete** breakdown |
| Forms **carbon dioxide and water** | Forms **alcohol and carbon dioxide** |
| **Much** energy | **Little** energy |

questions.solution_md: Oxygen; breakdown; products; energy.

questions.solution_md: Fermentation; carbon dioxide and alcohol; no oxygen.

questions.stem_md:
A farmer's field floods and the roots of the crop are under water for a week, with almost no air. A student reads that aerobic respiration releases 36 units of energy and anaerobic respiration 2 units for each glucose molecule.

(a) Name the type of respiration that the roots will mainly carry out and give a reason. [2]

(b) Name the end products and state how they differ from those of aerobic respiration. [2]

(c) Calculate the energy released from 12 glucose molecules by anaerobic respiration. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a cell showing where glycolysis and the Krebs cycle take place, with four labels. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Anaerobic respiration**, because there is **little or no oxygen**.

**(b)** **Alcohol and carbon dioxide**; aerobic respiration forms **carbon dioxide and water**.

**(c)** 12 × 2 = **24 units**.

**(d)** A **cell** with **cytoplasm** (glycolysis) and a **mitochondrion** (Krebs cycle), with arrows for **glucose** and **pyruvate**. Four labels.

questions.solution_md: Anaerobic, no oxygen; alcohol and carbon dioxide; 24 units; labelled cell.

marking_scheme.step: Cell with cytoplasm and mitochondrion drawn

questions.stem_md:
A leaf patch has 1200 stomata, of which 900 are open in bright light. A student also notes that the bark of a tree has small raised pores and that the roots of the same tree absorb oxygen from the soil.

(a) Calculate how many stomata are closed. [2]

(b) Name the pores in the bark and state how roots get oxygen. [2]

(c) State the process by which gases move through these openings. [1]

(d) Explain why a green plant gives out carbon dioxide at night but not by day. [2]

(e) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the control flask Y of the carbon dioxide experiment, naming three parts. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 1200 − 900 = **300**.

**(b)** The pores are **lenticels**; roots take **oxygen from air spaces in the soil** through root hairs and surface cells.

**(c)** **Diffusion**.

**(d)** At night only **respiration** goes on, giving out carbon dioxide; by day **photosynthesis uses it**, in greater amounts than respiration releases.

**(e)** A **flask** with **boiled seeds**, a **cork** and **delivery tube** into **lime water**. Three labels.

questions.solution_md: 300 closed; lenticels, oxygen from soil air; diffusion; night and day; labelled flask Y.

marking_scheme.step: Roots take oxygen from soil air
